item.title: Maastricht and son of André Rieu at odds over Christmas decor
item.description:
Maastricht and son of André Rieu at odds over Christmas decor

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Maastricht has limited how Pierre Rieu can decorate his hotel in the city center, telling the son of famous musician André Rieu that his current proposal is too extravagant.

Rieu had proposed to turn the historic building into a life-sized Christmas gift, with string lights and an illuminated bow.

The 4-star Hotel Derlon dates from 1870 and was bought by Rieu in 2025.

He had done up the hotel in the same manner last year, but the city’s Planning and Monuments Commission found the decorations to be excessive, according to local news outlet L1.

The hotelier was told he needed to choose between the bow and the string lights to allow the building’s architecture to be visible.

Rieu told regional broadcaster 1Zuid he was irritated with the decision. “We’re talking about Christmas lights. I don’t think anyone is bothered by that,” he said.

item.title: More Dutch students studying abroad, Spain most popular choice
item.description:
More Dutch students studying abroad, Spain most popular choice

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

More Dutch students are spending part of their degree abroad, but the proportion is still below pre-pandemic levels, according to latest official figures.

Some 24% of students who graduated from universities and vocational colleges in 2025 went abroad for part of their studies, with one in six (17%) staying for three months or longer.

Five years ago, during the most restricted phase of the coronavirus pandemic, just 16% of all students had spent time outside the Netherlands, the government statistics agency CBS said.

Spain was the most popular destination for students who took part in the Erasmus+ exchange programme between 2014 and 2024, accounting 16.9% of the total, followed by Germany (9.7%) and the UK (8.9%).

The last figure is noteworthy because Britain left the Erasmus+ scheme in 2020 as part of the Brexit agreement, though it is rejoining from next year.

Students who went abroad for their entire degree were most likely to go to Belgium, followed by the UK and the United States.

Online decline

One in seven students took part in online lessons or projects hosted by foreign colleges and universities, but here there was a declining trend, particularly among university students.

Just 10% of the latter group followed an online course, down from 14% in 2021, while for vocational students the proportion slipped from 19% to 18%.

More than one-third (36%) of recent graduates who spent time abroad also included an online element.

item.title: LGBT tolerance slumps in the Netherlands as debate turns vicious
item.description:
LGBT tolerance slumps in the Netherlands as debate turns vicious

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Less than a quarter of schoolboys in the Netherlands have a positive view of homosexuality, almost half the proportion of four years ago, according to a Europe-wide survey.

The HBSC (Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children) poll found that just 22% of boys aged 12 to 16 had a positive view of homosexuality, compared to 40% the last time the survey was carried out in 2021.

Gonneke Stevens, professor of Social and Behavioural Sciences at Utrecht University, said there was a “worrying turn in the trend” after decades of growing acceptance of same-sex relationships.

“In recent years sexual diversity has been increasingly questioned by leading figures in society, including politicians,” said Stevens, who led the Dutch research team in collaboration with the Trimbos mental health institute.

The COC, which campaigns for LGBGTI rights in the Netherlands, described the findings as a “frightening development.” Director Marie Ricardo said: “We badly need the young generation for a free country in which everyone can be themselves.”

The survey found girls were still more accepting of homosexuality than boys, but the proportion had fallen from 78% to just over half (51%) since 2021.

Manosphere

Stevens said there was a clear link between deepening intolerance and the rise of trends on social media such as the “manosphere”, which provides a platform for aggressive and discriminatory messages about women and gays.

“The fact is that in recent years young people have been exposed to these views and that in the same period they have taken a more negative view of homosexuality.”

Hardline conservative organisations have also pushed back against efforts to promote tolerance in education by promoting spurious links between homosexuality and paedophilia.

In 2023 children’s writer Pim Lammers had to go into hiding after receiving death threats when his novel De Boer en de Dierenarts (“The farmer and the vet”), about a same-sex relationship, was targeted by the radical Catholic organisation Civitas Christiana after he was asked to write a poem for children’s book week.

The sex education institute Rutgers, which organises the annual “Week van de Lentekriebels” (Spring Fever Week), won a court case against Civitas Christiana banning it from making false statements or publishing its “black book”, listing people and organisations that it accuses of “sexualising” children. The judgment was upheld by the Court of Appeal in May.

item.title: The week will be sunny, with a bit of rain and highs of 21C

The week will be sunny, with a bit of rain and highs of 21C

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Netherlands will see a mix of sun and clouds in the coming days, with a bit of rain midweek, but warm temperatures and sunshine are predicted for the weekend.

The Dutch meteorological institute KNMI says Monday will mostly be cloudy and dry, with highs ranging from from 17°C in the north to 21°C in the southeast.

Tuesday will be cloudy, with a chance of light rain, with highs of 16°C to 21°C across the country.

Wednesday and Thursday will be wet. The KNMI says there is a 60-70% chance of rain midweek, with the occasional break of sun.

The weekend is likely to be warm, with highs on Sunday reaching 23°C.

item.title: Meerdink and Til added to Oranje Nations League squad
item.description:
Meerdink and Til added to Oranje Nations League squad

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

AZ Alkmaar striker Mexx Meerdink and PSV’s Guus Til have been called up as late replacements to Xavi Hernandez’ Netherlands men’s football squad for this week’s Nations League clash with Germany.

They replace Bournemouth striker Justin Kluivert and AS Roma forward Donyell Malen, who withdrew at the weekend with injuries.

Til, 28, has won eight caps in as many years and was part of Ronald Koeman’s World Cup squad in the summer, marked his recall by scoring twice for his club away to Twente Enschede at the weekend, but PSV still lost 3-2.

Meerdink, 23, who is hiping to win his first cap, scored AZ’s only goal against Telstar as they leapfrogged PSV at the top of the table.

The inclusion of the pair brings the number of Eredivisie players in Xavi’s 26-man squad to five. Thursday’s match against Germany in Amsterdam is the Spaniard’s first as head coach since he was appointed as Koeman’s successor last month.

item.title: Jetten condemns second year of far-right riots in The Hague
item.description:
Jetten condemns second year of far-right riots in The Hague

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Prime minister Rob Jetten has condemned rioters who clashed with police for the second year in a row at a demonstration in The Hague organised by the far right.

Police broke up the gathering of around 300 people on the Malieveld on Saturday afternoon on the orders of acting mayor Richard de Mos.

Altogether 24 people were arrested for ignoring an emergency order to disperse and carrying weapons. All of them were released on Sunday pending further inquiries.

“They thew fireworks at police, committed vandalism and wore face-covering clothing, despite an agreement with the organisers that they would not,” a spokesman said.

Jetten said in a post on X that the rioters had “deliberately sought to confront police”. He added that they “used excessive violence against police, chanted repulsive extreme-right and anti-Semitic slogans and made Nazi salutes”.

March cancelled

A far-right group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”) organised Saturday’s demonstration against immigration. The violence was less extreme than a year ago, when 1,000 rioters set fire to police cars, blockaded the A12 motorway and smashed windows at the offices of Jetten’s party D66.

Op het Malieveld is vandaag door relschoppers bewust de confrontatie gezocht met de politie. Er is excessief geweld tegen de politie gebruikt, er zijn weerzinwekkende extreemrechtse en antisemitische uitingen gescandeerd en Hitlergroeten gebracht.

Veel waardering voor het…

— Rob Jetten (@MinPres) September 19, 2026

Originally the group was due to march through the city, but De Mos cancelled the march after some members refused to remove face masks.

“That is why we cancelled the march and only allowed a demonstration on the Malieveld,” the acting mayor said. “When the violence continued, it was necessary to put an end to it.”

Photographer in water

A Spanish photographer who was covering the demonstration filed an official complaint against police after he was allegedly pushed into a canal by an officer.

Nacho Calogne, who works as a freelance correspondent, told NOS his accreditation was clearly visible. “Not one police officer came over afterwards to help me or check if I was OK,” he said. “Other photographers pulled me out.”

Police said they had made contact with the photographer and the Dutch journalists’ union NVJ to discuss possible compensation.

Three other journalists reported they were intimidated and attacked during the demonstration, according to PersVeilig, which campaigns for the safety of reporters.

item.title: Police have identified shooters in deadly Overasselt attack
item.description:
Police have identified shooters in deadly Overasselt attack

September 21, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police have determined which two men were directly involved in the killing of a security guard during the deadly attack in Overasselt earlier this month, according to De Telegraaf.

Police arrested 35 people after a group of armed men descended on the village in Gelderland in the early hours of September 1 and opened fire on a farmhouse, killing the 51-year-old guard and seriously injuring two police officers.

CCTV footage showed dozens of masked men getting out of a truck outside the property, some heavily armed, before one shoots a man sitting in a car.

They also opened fire on police responding to the scene, injuring two.

It is suspected the attack was part of a feud over cocaine dealing linked with the man living in the farmhouse, Jan G., who had been targeted previously.

At the weekend, German police detained a 28-year-old man in a car park near the Dutch border on suspicion of trying to smuggle nearly four tonnes of cocaine through the French port of Dunkirk.

According to the NOS, that man was Jan G., who had been banned from the Overasselt for three months following the violence.

The men arrested in the wake of the shooting were of varying nationalities, including Dutch, French, Algerian and Belgian. Six were from the Amsterdam area. Some were caught while hiding in fields or trying to flee the area by car or train.

Judges have ordered all but one of the suspects to be detained in custody for the next three months while investigations continue.

item.title: AZ top Eredivisie after Twente stage late comeback against PSV
item.description:
AZ top Eredivisie after Twente stage late comeback against PSV

September 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

AZ Alkmaar go into the international break as Eredivisie league leaders after PSV were hit by two late goals at Twente to suffer their first defeat of the season.

The champions suffered an early blow when striker Ricardo Pepi limped off with an injury after nine minutes.

Twente dominated the first 20 minutes and could have had more to show for it than Younes Taha’s opportunistic strike. But two quick goals by stand-in striker Guus Til turned the match around just before the half-hour mark.

PSV surrendered their lead when Wout Weghorst sprung a poorly set offside trap before finishing coolly. And eight minutes from time French midfielder Daouida Weidmann ran all the way from the halfway line and steered the ball around Matej Kovar for the winner.

Ronald Koeman Jr. did his best to deny AZ Alkmaar victory in the Noord-Holland derby, but was unable to keep out Mexx Meerdinck’s 19th-minute shot. AZ were denied a second when Meerdinck handled the ball just before squaring it to Kees Smit.

Feyenoord rampant

Feyenoord moved up to second place with another salvo of goals, including a double for Anis Hadj-Moussa, against struggling Utrecht to take their tally for the season to 25 in just seven matches.

Julian Brandt scored for the third match in a row for Ajax, but the Amsterdammers could only manage a draw at home against Excelsior despite having 33 shots on target.

The Rottterdam club took a 2-1 lead when Aymen Sliti finished off a flowing move in the 62nd minute, but two minutes later summer loan signing Tolu Arokodare showed his strength to tap in an equaliser.

Fortuna Sittard kept up their good start to the season as Philip Brittijn’s late goal was enough to send Willem II to the bottom of the table.

Groningen cruised to a 3-0 win against PEC Zwolle, who were still smarting from last week’s 7-0 drubbing by Feyenoord.

Heerenveen hit four goals against Sparta to record their first win since the opening day of the season, while NEC’s rocky start to the season continued as they could only manage a home draw against Go Ahead Eagles.

In the battle of the newly promoted clubs, ADO Den Haag picked up a precious point at home to Cambuur Leeuwarden to lift themselves off the bottom of the table as Donát Bárány equalised in the 74th minute.

item.title: Arrests after far-right protesters attack police in The Hague
item.description:
Arrests after far-right protesters attack police in The Hague

September 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Police have made 24 arrests in The Hague after an anti-immigration march in The Hague organised by a far-right group turned violent.

Several hundred people gathered at the site near Centraal Station at around 11am after a group calling itself Wij Zijn Het Volk (“We are the people”) announced the event, exactly a year after a similar demonstration descended into a full-blown riot.

Protesters wearing balaclavas, scarves and masks to cover their faces gave Nazi salutes and carried banners with racist slogans such as “remigratie” (remig “blanke mannen vooraan” (“white men first”).

Acting mayor Richard de Mos ordered riot police to clear the Malieveld after demonstrators attacked police and ignored earlier orders to remove face coverings.

The rioters threw smoke bombs and fireworks and ripped traffic poles out of the ground, at least one of which was hurled at police. Police beat back the crowd towards Centraal Station using dogs, pepper spray and batons, managing to restore order by 3.30pm.

However, the violence was less extreme than a year ago, when 1,000 rioters set fire to police cars, blockaded the A12 motorway and smashed windows at the offices of political party D66.

“Atrocious”

Justice minister David van Weel called the scenes “atrocious” in a post on social media site X, while De Mos said the violence directed at police “crossed a line”.

“Hitler salutes, anti-Semitic chants, violence against police and fireworks thrown at riot squad officers,” Van Weel said. “It’s important that these people are dealt with severely.”

“That is why we cancelled the march and only allowed a demonstration on the Malieveld,” De Mos said. “When the violence continued, it was necessary to put an end to it.”

Walgelijke beelden vanaf het Malieveld. Hitlergroeten, antisemitische leuzen, geweld tegen de politie en vuurwerk gooien naar de ME. Belangrijk dat hier snoeihard tegen opgetreden wordt. Dank aan alle agenten die weer voor onze rechtsstaat staan.https://t.co/31JadLNBjJ

— David van Weel (@ministerjenv) September 19, 2026

item.title: Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht
item.description:
Dutch destinations: Check out the highs and lows of Maastricht

September 19, 2026 Molly Quell

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

One of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, Maastricht lies in the southern part of the country, close to both the Belgian and German borders. It is no wonder that the founding treaty of the European Union was signed there, nor that the Belgian (and French) influence has created a food mecca.

No one can quite agree on its exact origins. Celts lived in the area at least as far back as the 5th century BC, and the Romans showed up about 600 years later to build a bridge over the Meuse River that now runs through the centre of the city. Maastricht played a vital role in the Carolingian Empire and the Holy Roman Empire, and its location made it quite coveted between the 16th and 18th centuries. Many of those fortifications are still standing.

It was the first Dutch city to be liberated by the Allies during World War II. Half-century later, the city hosted a series of councils that led to the signing of the Maastricht Treaty, which paved the way toward the establishment of the European Union and the euro.

Maastricht is now home for 125,000 people, including many of the students studying at nearby Maastricht University.

Five things to do

Enjoy the city’s long and storied past with a historic walk.

Start at the Vrijthof, the main square where Dutch conductor André Rieu holds his summer concert series and which turns into a Christmas market in the winter.

Vrijthof is home to the majestic Basilica of Saint Servatius, where Maastricht’s patron saint Servatius is said to have died in 384 AD. A stone church was built over his grave in the 6th century which has been gradually expanded to the looming structure you see today.

You can loop past Our Lady, Star of the Sea (Sterre der Zee), a popular pilgrimage site, and see the famous wooden statue of Mary that dates to the 15th century.

Walk under the Helpoort (Hell’s Gate), the oldest city gate in the whole of the Netherlands, and then stroll through the Stadspark. On a nice day, you can join the many students who spread out a blanket and enjoy a few beers in the sun.

The part is also home to a number of sculptures and art installations. You can walk along the city walls and even see a statue of the fourth musketeer d’Artagnan. The leader of King Louis XIV’s elite corps of gentlemen, died in battle in 1673 during the French siege of Maastricht and archaeologists recently announced they may have discovered his skeletal remains under the floorboards of a nearby church.

If you want to go deeper into history, go underground
You can tour the caves of Mount Saint Peter, a collection of limestone quarries which date back to the 13th century. During World War II, they were used to safeguard arms and valuables from the Germans, including The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn which was removed from its frame and rolled into a cylinder.

You can also walk through the casemates (kazematten), defensive corridors that run under the city. These structures are unique in the Netherlands, as the groundwater level is too high in other parts of the country.

Visit a bookstore
The 700-year-old Dominicanenkerk has quite the history. Along with serving as a house of worship, the church has been used as a warehouse, an archive, a printing house, and even a place to store bikes. Napoleon used it to store equipment and military personnel while invading the region in the 1790s.

It was converted into one of Europe’s most unique bookstores following a restoration project in the mid 2000s. If that’s not enough, you can also check out De Tribune, which was named the best literary bookstore in the Netherlands in 2024.

Shop til you drop
Maastricht is known for its shopping and the city is filled with boutiques, art galleries, vintage shops and more. The Rechtstraat is just one of many lovely shopping streets. On Wednesday and Fridays, the city holds a market with Friday wares more orientated towards clothing. On Saturday, hundreds of vendors turn out for the antiques market.

Go to the other extreme
Just outside Maastricht, you can find the highest point in the Netherlands. At a little over 322 metres tall, the Vaalserberg might merely be considered an average hill in other countries, but for the Netherlands, that’s a mountain.

It’s also home to Drielandenpunt, a three country-point where the borders of Belgium, Germany, and the Netherlands meet. Its lookout towers offer great views of the surrounding region.

Where to eat

Limburgse vlaai is the local delicacy and a must have on any trip to Maastricht. It’s not quite a pie and it’s not quite a pastry, but it’s definitely delicious. De Bisschopsmolen currently has no less than nine on the menu at their bakery and cafe. If you’d like to try your hand at making your own, they also host vlaai workshops.

The Onze Lieve Vrouweplein has a collection of outdoor cafes where you can enjoy a coffee or a beer.

If you want a fancy meal, look to L’Auberge. This lovely restaurant sits in the former stables of Château Neercanne. For an even fancier meal, the companion Restaurant Château Neercanne. For a real treat, you can stay at the hotel.

Cycle outside of the city and have lunch at Grand-Café Buitengoed Slavante. The country estate has a great breakfast menu and you can also take a walk on the grounds.

Another great lunch option in the city is the hip, Marres Kitchen. It’s in the same building as the museum Marres, House for Contemporary Culture so enjoy some art at the same time.

Where to stay

For a boutique experience, try Townhouse Hotel Maastricht. It also offers apartments if you’d like to eat your vlaai at home. Kruisherenhotel is the only five star hotel in the region. It’s housed in a 15th century monastery along the Kommelplein and each one of its 60 guest rooms features unique art and decor. The the Easy Hotel is a clean and cheap choice.

How to get there

The train stops practically in the middle of the city and you can walk in along a beautifully landscaped boulevard. It’s about three hours from Amsterdam. The drive is a bit shorter, at 2.5 hours, depending on the traffic.

Anything else

Keep in mind that Maastricht is south of the river and therefore deep into Carnival territory. Andre Rieu’s summer concerts are extremely popular and thus make it impossible to find hotels and parking.
